rocks.name: Hematite "blueberries"
rocks.fact: Tiny grey balls, smaller than peas, scattered all over the ground. They are made of a mineral called hematite.
rocks.why: They formed when water soaked through the rocks long ago. They were one of the first big clues that Meridiani was once wet.

rocks.name: Basalt
rocks.fact: Dark rock that formed when lava from volcanoes cooled down.
rocks.why: Most of Mars's surface is basalt. It tells us Mars had lots of volcanoes, including Olympus Mons, the biggest volcano we know of.

rocks.name: Salty sandstone (Burns formation)
rocks.fact: Pale rock made of sand grains glued together with salts, in thin layers like the pages of a book.
rocks.why: The layers were laid down by wind and shallow, salty water. Reading them is like reading Mars's diary.

rocks.name: Jarosite
rocks.fact: A yellow-brown mineral that only forms in water.
rocks.why: Finding jarosite proved there was liquid water here long ago. The water was very acidic, like lemon juice.

rocks.name: Lake mudstone
rocks.where: Yellowknife Bay, Gale crater (the rock 'John Klein')
rocks.fact: Rock made from fine mud that settled at the bottom of an old lake.
rocks.why: Curiosity drilled it and found the chemical ingredients that tiny life could use. Gale crater once had a lake that could have been a home for microbes.

rocks.name: Gypsum vein (Homestake)
rocks.fact: A bright white stripe of a mineral called gypsum, filling a crack in the rock.
rocks.why: Water flowed through the crack and left the gypsum behind. This water was gentler than the acidic water that made jarosite.

rocks.name: Silica-rich soil
rocks.where: Next to Home Plate, Gusev crater
rocks.fact: Bright, almost pure white soil. Spirit found it by accident when its broken wheel dug a trench!
rocks.why: Soil this rich in silica forms near hot springs or steam vents. On Earth, places like that are full of microbes.

rocks.name: Carbonate rock (Comanche)
rocks.where: Comanche outcrop, Columbia Hills, Gusev crater
rocks.fact: A rock with lots of carbonate minerals (like the chalk and limestone we have on Earth).
rocks.why: Carbonates dissolve in acid, so these formed in water that was not acidic: a friendlier place for life.

rocks.name: Clay rock (Esperance)
rocks.fact: A pale rock changed into clay minerals by lots of water flowing through it.
rocks.why: Scientists called it some of the best evidence for drinkable, neutral water that Opportunity ever found.

rocks.name: Iron meteorite (Heat Shield Rock)
rocks.where: Meridiani Planum, next to Opportunity's own heat shield
rocks.fact: A shiny lump of iron and nickel the size of a basketball that fell from space.
rocks.why: It was the first meteorite ever found on another planet!

rocks.name: Iron meteorite (Block Island)
rocks.fact: A big iron meteorite, about the size of a large watermelon.
rocks.why: For an iron rock this big to land without burning up or smashing, Mars's air may have been thicker long ago.

rocks.name: Leopard-spot rock (Cheyava Falls)
rocks.where: Jezero crater, an ancient river valley
rocks.fact: A reddish rock covered in tiny pale spots with dark rims, like a leopard's coat.
rocks.why: On Earth, spots like these can be made by microbes. They might be a sign of ancient life, but scientists need more tests (maybe on Earth) to know for sure.
